note: Parallel run; per-subagent wall clock, not human approval time.

a.keyRule: Discount percent is capped at 30; anything above 30 is not allowed.
a.counterexample: function discount(price, percent) { return Math.max(0, price * (1 - percent / 100)); }
reasons: The only case is percent 10 -> total 90, which the counterexample satisfies.
The only property is total >= 0, which Math.max(0, ...) satisfies for any percent.
No precondition caps percent at 30 and no case exercises percent above 30, so a 50 percent or 100 percent discount is accepted despite the sentence.

b.keyRule: discount percent must be at most 30 (upper limit)
b.counterexample: function discount(price, percent) { return Math.max(0, price * (1 - percent / 100)); }
reasons: The only case is percent 10, which is below the limit, so it never exercises the 30% bound.

The percent precondition is only gte 0, with no upper bound, and the floor property only requires total >= 0; the counterexample (no cap, clamped at 0) satisfies both, so percent 50 or 100 is accepted though the sentence caps discounts at 30.

a.keyRule: Reject when amount > balance (strictly above available balance).
a.counterexample: function purchase(balance, amount){ if (amount >= balance + 50) return {status:'REJECTED', balance_unchanged:true, balance_after:balance}; return {status:'ACCEPTED', balance_unchanged:false, balance_after:Math.max(0, balance-amount)}; }
reasons: Only one case (balance 100, amount 150); the only property is balance_after >= 0.

The counterexample rejects only when amount exceeds balance by 50 or more, accepting overdrafts such as balance 100, amount 120, yet matches the case and clamps balance_after to >= 0 so the floor property still holds.
No case or property pins the boundary or any ACCEPTED/REJECTED outcome for smaller overages.

b.keyRule: Reject when amount is strictly greater than the available balance (amount > balance); a purchase at or below balance is not rejected.
b.counterexample: function purchase(balance, amount){ return {status:'REJECTED', balance_unchanged:true, balance_after:balance}; }
reasons: Always rejecting returns the expected values for the only case (100,150) and keeps balance_after >= 0, so it satisfies the floor property; likewise rejecting when amount >= balance passes.
No case requires ACCEPTED for an amount at or below the balance, so the 'above' boundary (strictly greater) is unpinned and the contract cannot distinguish over-rejecting implementations.

a.keyRule: Ties (x.5) round up; non-ties round to nearest
reasons: Only case is 1.5 -> 2; Math.ceil returns 2 and is >= 0 so the floor property holds, yet 1.2 -> 2 breaks 'round'.
Banker's rounding (round half to even) also passes: 1.5 -> 2, but 2.5 -> 2 breaks 'half up'. No case distinguishes half-up from half-even.

b.keyRule: Ties (x.5) round up, not to even or elsewhere
b.counterexample: function round(value){ const f=Math.floor(value), d=value-f; if(d===0.5) return f%2===0?f:f+1; return Math.round(value); }
reasons: Only case is 1.5 -> 2, which round-half-to-even also yields; 2.5 would give 2 instead of 3 and no case or property detects it.
The floor property (min 0) is satisfied by any non-negative output.

a.keyRule: attempts is capped at 3 (min(requested, 3))
reasons: The only case (requested=1 -> attempts=1) and the floor property (attempts >= 0) are satisfied by an uncapped implementation that returns requested, so the limit of 3 is never exercised.
Secondary: 'retry at most 3 times' could mean 3 retries (4 attempts) or 3 attempts; no case or limitation names the choice.

b.keyRule: at most 3 retries (upper cap of 3)
reasons: The only case (requested 1 -> attempts 1) and the floor property (attempts >= 0) are satisfied by an uncapped implementation that returns requested, so the limit of 3 is never exercised.
Hidden ambiguity: 'at most 3 retries' could mean 3 retries (4 attempts) or 3 attempts; the observable is 'attempts' and limitations does not name the choice.

a.keyRule: When matches is 0 the filter returns no products (count 0).
reasons: The only input is matches, and the case none pins matches 0 to count 0, which is exactly the sentence's rule.
Any implementation that breaks the rule must return count > 0 for matches 0, which the case rejects; no counterexample exists.
Template parts (floor, gte 0, limitations) are not grounds for rejection.

b.keyRule: When the filter matches nothing (matches = 0), the result contains no products (count = 0).
reasons: The only rule is matches=0 -> count=0; the case 'none' pins exactly that, so any implementation returning nonzero there fails.
The sentence says nothing about matches>0, so no implementation can violate the rule while passing the case.
No contradiction or ambiguity between sentence, case and floor property.

a.keyRule: A user sees exactly their own orders (visible = own, excluding others').
reasons: The only case (own=1, others=4 -> visible=1) is satisfied by returning min(own,1), which drops own orders when own>1; the floor property (>=0) also holds.
No case pins visible to own for values other than 1, so the rule that all own orders are visible is not enforced.

b.keyRule: A user sees their own orders, and only their own (visible equals own, never including others' orders).
reasons: The only case (own=1, others=4 -> visible=1) is also satisfied by returning min(own,1), which drops own orders beyond one; the floor property only requires visible >= 0.
No case varies own above 1 or checks that all own orders are visible, so under-showing own orders passes.
An implementation returning own + others when own is 1... is excluded by the case, but one returning others > 0 ? 1 : own also passes while ignoring the real rule.

a.keyRule: fee = max(2% of price, 1): percentage above the minimum, floor of 1 below it
reasons: The only case (price 10 -> fee 1) lands on the minimum branch, so the 2% rule is never exercised.
The only property is fee >= 0, which a constant 1 satisfies; the 2% charge for large prices is unconstrained.

b.keyRule: fee = max(2% of price, 1): 2% rate applies above the minimum
reasons: The only case (price 10 -> fee 1) is the minimum branch (2% of 10 = 0.2 < 1), so the 2% rate is never exercised.
Constant fee 1 passes the case and the floor property (min 0), yet ignores the 2% rule for price > 50.

a.keyRule: Delivery span counts only business days: calendar days minus weekend days.
reasons: The only case (calendar 3, weekend 2 -> days 1) is satisfied by calendar-2, which ignores the weekend input and subtracts a constant, or by a constant 1.
The floor property only requires days >= 0 and does not pin the weekend subtraction, so a wrong rule passes every case and property.

b.keyRule: Only business days are counted: result = calendar days minus weekend days.
b.counterexample: function delivery_span({calendar, weekend}) { return Math.max(0, calendar - 2); }
reasons: Single case (calendar 3, weekend 2 -> 1) is satisfied by ignoring the weekend input and subtracting a constant 2; floor property (>=0) holds via Math.max.
No case or property ties the output to the weekend input, so an implementation can ignore it and still pass.

a.keyRule: length >= 8 (inclusive threshold at 8)
reasons: Only case is length 9, so an implementation using strict > 8 (rejecting exactly 8) passes it.
No case pins the boundary at 8 and the floor property only bounds seen >= 0, so the 'at least' inclusive boundary is unchecked.

b.keyRule: Threshold: length >= 8 is accepted (8 is the boundary)
b.counterexample: function password(length){ return { accepted: length >= 9, seen: length }; }
reasons: The only case is length 9 -> accepted true, so any threshold at or below 9 passes it; the sentence's boundary of 8 is never exercised.
No case for length 8 (accepted) or 7 (rejected); floor property only bounds seen >= 0, so >= 9 satisfies every case and property while rejecting an 8-character password.

a.keyRule: sold never exceeds stock (sold = min(stock, requested))
a.counterexample: function sell(stock, requested){ return (stock===2 && requested===5) ? 2 : requested; }
reasons: Only one case (stock 2, requested 5 -> 2) and the floor property (sold >= 0) exist; nothing bounds sold by stock, so an implementation returning requested in all other inputs (e.g. stock 1, requested 5 -> 5) oversells yet passes every case and property.

b.keyRule: sold must never exceed stock on hand (sold <= stock)
b.counterexample: function sell(stock, requested) { return stock === 2 ? Math.min(stock, requested) : requested; }
reasons: The only case is stock 2, requested 5 -> sold 2; the only property is sold >= 0. Nothing bounds sold above by stock, so selling requested when stock is not 2 (e.g. stock 1, requested 5 -> 5) passes everything while overselling.

a.keyRule: Order: the first matching coupon is applied, not a later or better one.
a.counterexample: function coupon(first, second) { return Math.max(first, second); }
reasons: The only case (first=10, second=5 -> 10) is also satisfied by max(first, second), which picks the best coupon rather than the first; the floor property (>= 0) also holds.
No case has a first coupon smaller than the second, so nothing pins the order rule.

b.keyRule: Order: the first matching coupon is applied, not another one (first takes precedence over second).
b.counterexample: function coupon(first, second) { return { discount: Math.max(first, second) }; }
reasons: The only case (first 10, second 5 -> 10) is also satisfied by picking the larger coupon, so it does not pin down 'first'.
The floor property (discount >= 0) holds for max given non-negative inputs.
No case where second > first, so first-vs-best is never distinguished.

a.keyRule: refund = price * (total - used) / total, i.e. only the unused fraction of the price
a.counterexample: function refund({price, used, total}) { return price * 0.75; }
reasons: The only case (price 100, used 1, total 4 -> 75) is satisfied by a constant 0.75 factor, ignoring used and total.
The floor property only requires refund >= 0, which the constant satisfies, so nothing pins the unused-days proportion.

b.keyRule: Refund is proportional to unused days: price * (total - used) / total
reasons: The only case (price 100, used 1, total 4 -> 75) is satisfied by a constant 75 or by price * 0.75 or price - 25 * used; the floor property (min 0) is also satisfied.
No case or property pins how the refund scales with price, used or total, so the unused-days rule is untested.

a.keyRule: Products are ordered by name
reasons: The only case (aId 2, bId 1 -> first a) is satisfied by always returning 'a'; the floor property only bounds seen >= 0.
Inputs are ids, not names, so the contract never ties the result to name order; it also fits an id-descending reading and limitations does not name the choice.

b.keyRule: Products are ordered by name (not by id or any other key)
b.counterexample: function sort({aId,bId}){ return { first: aId > bId ? 'a' : 'b', seen: 0 }; }
reasons: No input carries a name; inputs are only aId and bId, so the contract cannot distinguish name order from id order.
The single case (aId 2, bId 1 -> first a) is satisfied by ordering by id descending, and the floor property (seen >= 0) is satisfied trivially.
Hidden ambiguity: how ids map to names is not stated and limitations does not name it.

a.keyRule: Registration is rejected whenever the email already exists (existing >= 1), otherwise accepted.
a.counterexample: function register({existing}){ return {status: existing === 1 ? 'REJECTED' : 'ACCEPTED', seen: existing}; }
reasons: The only case is existing=1 -> REJECTED; an implementation that rejects only when existing===1 passes it.
The only property is the seen floor (min 0), which says nothing about status, so existing=2 or more being ACCEPTED violates the sentence yet passes everything.

b.keyRule: A register call is rejected only when the email already exists (existing > 0); otherwise it is accepted.
reasons: The only case is existing=1 -> REJECTED; an implementation that always returns REJECTED (even for existing=0) satisfies it and the floor property (seen>=0).
No case pins ACCEPTED for a non-duplicate, so over-rejection is undetected.

a.keyRule: When the payment call times out, the result is the fallback value.
a.counterexample: function payment_fetch({wait}) { return { value: wait === 100 ? 'fallback' : 'error', seen: 0 }; }
reasons: The only case is wait=100 -> fallback. An implementation that returns fallback only for wait exactly 100 and error otherwise passes the case and the bounded_output floor, yet fails to return the fallback for longer waits (e.g. 5000) that are also timeouts.
No case or property pins what counts as a timeout or that larger waits also yield the fallback, and limitations does not name this choice.

b.keyRule: Only when the payment fetch times out, return the fallback (timeout is the condition that triggers the fallback).
reasons: The only case (wait 100 -> fallback) and the floor property (seen >= 0) are satisfied by an implementation that returns the fallback unconditionally, so the 'on timeout' condition is never exercised.
No case shows a non-timeout wait returning something other than fallback, and no timeout threshold is defined, so the condition is untested and the threshold is not named in limitations.

a.keyRule: total = price plus tax computed from price and rate (price*(1+rate/100))
a.counterexample: function total(price, rate) { return price + rate; }
reasons: The only case (price 100, rate 10, total 110) is satisfied by adding rate flat to price; the floor property (total >= 0) also holds, so the tax computation is never pinned down.
Rate is also ambiguous as percent vs fraction; the case fits only percent, and limitations does not name the choice.

b.keyRule: total = price plus tax computed from price and rate (tax scales with price)
b.counterexample: function total(price, rate){ return price + rate; }
reasons: The only case (price 100, rate 10 -> 110) is also satisfied by price + rate, which ignores that tax is a function of price; the floor property (min 0) also holds.
Rate meaning (percent vs fraction) is also only pinned by one case, so a single data point cannot distinguish tax = price*rate/100 from tax = rate.

a.keyRule: Threshold: age strictly under 12 pays half the fare; age 12 and above pays full.
a.counterexample: function ticket_price(age, fare){ return age <= 10 ? fare/2 : fare; }
reasons: The only case is age 10 / fare 100 -> 50, so the 12 threshold is never exercised; the counterexample uses a threshold of 10, passes the case and the non-negative floor property.
No case at ages 11 or 12, so the boundary (under 12 vs 12 or over) is unpinned, and age 11 would be charged full.

b.keyRule: Age threshold: children under 12 (age < 12) pay half the fare, otherwise full fare
b.counterexample: function ticket_price(age, fare) { return age <= 10 ? fare / 2 : fare; }
reasons: Only case is age 10, fare 100 -> 50; it does not probe the threshold at 12, so a wrong cutoff (e.g. age <= 10 or age < 11) passes.
The floor property (due >= 0) is satisfied by any non-negative output including the counterexample.
Ages 11 would be charged full fare by the counterexample, violating 'under 12', yet every case and property passes.

a.keyRule: On equal scores the leader wins (not the challenger).
a.counterexample: function rank(leader, challenger) { if (leader === 5 && challenger === 5) return { winner: 'leader', seen: 0 }; return { winner: challenger >= leader ? 'challenger' : 'leader', seen: 0 }; }
reasons: The only case is a tie at 5/5, so an implementation can special-case it and hand every other tie to the challenger.
No property constrains winner; the floor property only bounds seen, so it cannot catch the broken rule for ties like 3/3.

b.keyRule: On equal scores the winner is the leader, not the challenger.
b.counterexample: function rank(leader, challenger){ if (leader === challenger) return leader === 5 ? 'leader' : 'challenger'; return leader > challenger ? 'leader' : 'challenger'; }
reasons: The only case ties at 5/5, so an implementation that keeps the leader only for that exact value passes the case and the floor property while breaking the rule for every other tie.
No property states tie behaviour for general equal inputs.

a.keyRule: Any negative qty (qty < 0) yields REJECTED
a.counterexample: function quantity(qty){ return { status: qty === -1 ? 'REJECTED' : 'ACCEPTED', seen: 0 }; }
reasons: The only case is qty=-1; an implementation rejecting only -1 returns REJECTED for it.
The only property is bounded_output seen>=0, which seen=0 satisfies.
Precondition allows qty from -100, so -2..-100 are in-domain negatives, yet no case covers them and the stub accepts them.

b.keyRule: Any negative qty must be rejected (status REJECTED)
b.counterexample: function quantity(qty){ return { status: qty === -1 ? 'REJECTED' : 'ACCEPTED', seen: 0 }; }
reasons: The only case is qty=-1; an implementation rejecting only -1 passes it and the floor property (seen >= 0) while accepting -2, -50, -0.5 etc.
No case or property covers any other negative value, nor the accepted side (non-negative).

a.keyRule: Purchase is allowed when used equals limit (inclusive boundary), and below it.
a.counterexample: function purchase_limit(used, limit) { return { allowed: used === limit, seen: used }; }
reasons: The only case is used=10, limit=10 -> allowed true; the function returns true there but also returns false for used=5, limit=10, which the sentence (limit inclusive, so under-limit is allowed) requires to be true.
No case covers used below limit and no property constrains allowed, so any implementation that is true only at equality passes.

b.keyRule: When used equals limit the purchase is allowed (allowed iff used <= limit).
b.counterexample: function purchase_limit(used, limit) { return { allowed: used < limit || (used === 10 && limit === 10), seen: used }; }
reasons: The only case pins used=10, limit=10; the sole property is the template floor on seen, so nothing constrains inclusivity at other values.
The counterexample passes the edge case and floor but returns allowed=false for used=5, limit=5, breaking 'inclusive'.
